rule.summary: The imperative is the verb form for instructions, requests, advice and warnings. German has three forms for the person you speak to: **du** (one friend), **ihr** (several friends) and **Sie** (formal, one or more people). The verb stands in **position 1**; *du* and *ihr* drop the pronoun, *Sie* keeps it. A *wir*-form (*Gehen wir!*) means *let's*. Add *bitte*, *mal* or *doch* to make a request softer.
rule.table:
| Infinitiv | du | ihr | Sie |
|---|---|---|---|
| kommen | komm(e)! | kommt! | kommen Sie! |
| warten | wart**e**! | wart**et**! | warten Sie! |
| fahren | fahr(e)! (no umlaut) | fahrt! | fahren Sie! |
| sprechen | spr**i**ch! | sprecht! | sprechen Sie! |
| lesen | l**ie**s! | lest! | lesen Sie! |
| anrufen | ruf(e) … **an**! | ruft … **an**! | rufen Sie … **an**! |
| sein | **sei**! | **seid**! | **seien** Sie! |
| haben | hab(e)! | habt! | haben Sie! |
steps: Choose the form for the person you speak to: one friend → *du*, several friends → *ihr*, formal → *Sie*.

*du*: take the present-tense *du*-form and remove *-st* and the pronoun: *du kommst → komm!* A final *-e* is optional (*komme!*), but it is required after stems in *-t/-d* and after consonant + *m/n*: *warte!, öffne!*
*du* with a vowel change: keep **e → i/ie** (*nimm!, lies!*) and add no *-e*; drop the umlaut of **a → ä / au → äu** (*fahr!, lauf!*).
*ihr*: the present-tense *ihr*-form without the pronoun: *ihr kommt → kommt!, ihr wartet → wartet!* (never a vowel change: *nehmt!, helft!*). *Sie*: infinitive + *Sie*: *Kommen Sie!*
Put the verb first. A separable prefix goes to the end (*Ruf mich an!*), and a reflexive pronoun follows the verb directly (*Setz dich!*). *sein* is irregular: *sei! – seid! – seien Sie!*
pitfalls: Keeping the *-st* of the *du*-form: ✗ *Kommst bitte!* → ✓ *Komm bitte!*
Keeping the umlaut: ✗ *Fähr langsam!* → ✓ *Fahr langsam!* Only *e → i/ie* stays in the imperative.
Losing the *e → i* change: ✗ *Nehm den Bus!* → ✓ *Nimm den Bus!* (*Nehm* and *Geb* are heard in speech, but they are not standard.)
Forgetting *Sie* in the formal form: ✗ *Warten bitte hier!* → ✓ *Warten Sie bitte hier!*
Not splitting a separable verb: ✗ *Anruf mich!* → ✓ *Ruf mich an!* The prefix always goes to the end.

items.explanation: Start from the *du*-form: *du kommst*. Remove *-st* and the pronoun → **Komm**. *her* (= towards the speaker) is the prefix of *herkommen* and goes to the end.

mistake.why: The *du*-imperative has no *-st* ending. Without the pronoun, *kommst* is not a command: the form is *Komm!*

examples.en: Please bring the book with you!

items.explanation: *du gehst* → remove *-st* → **Geh**. The verb stands in position 1 and the pronoun *du* disappears. *Gehe!* is also correct, but in spoken German the short form is normal.

mistake.why: *gehst* is the present-tense form and needs the subject *du*. The command form drops *-st*: *Geh nach Hause!*

examples.en: Take the parcel to the post office!

items.explanation: The *ihr*-imperative is the present-tense form without the pronoun: *ihr hört zu → **Hört** … zu!* *zuhören* is separable, so *zu* goes to the end. *zuhören* takes a Dativ: *mir*.

mistake.why: A separable prefix never stays on the verb in position 1. It goes to the end: *Hört mir bitte zu!*

items.explanation: The formal imperative is the infinitive in position 1, followed by *Sie*: **Warten** Sie! The pronoun *Sie* must stay; without it the form is not an imperative.

mistake.why: *warte* is the *du*-form. With *Sie* the verb is always the infinitive: *Warten Sie!*

items.explanation: *essen* changes *e → i* in the *du*-form: *du isst*. The imperative keeps the change and drops *-t*: **Iss**. Verbs with *e → i* never take the optional *-e*.

mistake.why: *essen* has the *e → i* change, and it stays in the *du*-imperative: *Iss!* A form with *-e* is not possible for these verbs.

items.explanation: *sprechen* has *e → i* in the *du*-form: *du sprichst*. Remove *-st* and keep the *i* → **Sprich**.

mistake.why: The *du*-imperative keeps the *e → i* change of the present tense: *du sprichst → sprich!*

items.explanation: *sein* has its own imperative forms. The *du*-form is **Sei** (not built from *du bist*). An adjective after it stays without an ending: *ruhig*.

mistake.why: The rule "*du*-form minus *-st*" does not work for *sein*. The imperative is irregular: *Sei!*

items.explanation: For a group of friends the imperative of *sein* is **Seid** – the same as the present tense *ihr seid*. Note the spelling with *d*; *seit* (since) is a different word.

mistake.why: *seien* is only used with *Sie* (*Seien Sie leise!*). For *ihr* the form is *Seid!*

items.explanation: *lesen* changes the vowel only for *du* and *er/sie/es* (*du liest*). The *ihr*-form has no change: *ihr lest* → **Lest**. The ending is the normal *ihr*-ending *-t*: les + t → *lest*.

mistake.why: *liest* has the vowel change of *du/er*. The *ihr*-form keeps the infinitive vowel: *Lest!*

items.explanation: *du machst zu* → remove *-st* → **Mach** … *zu*. The verb comes first, and the prefix *zu* goes to the end of the sentence.

mistake.why: The separable prefix is split off in the imperative and moves to the end: *Mach die Tür zu!*

items.de: {{c1::Geben::to give · Sie}} Sie mir bitte den Stift!
items.explanation: The formal imperative is always the infinitive + *Sie*, so the *e → i* change of *geben* does not appear: **Geben** Sie! The Dativ *mir* comes before the Akkusativ noun *den Stift*.

mistake.why: Without *Sie* the infinitive is not a polite command. The formal imperative needs *Sie* after the verb: *Geben Sie mir …*

examples.de: Zeigen Sie mir bitte den Weg!
Bringen Sie mir bitte die Rechnung!

items.explanation: *ihr ruft an* → drop *ihr* → **Ruft** … *an*. The object *mich* and the time *morgen* stand between the verb and the prefix, which goes to the end.

mistake.why: *anrufen* is separable. In the imperative the prefix *an* goes to the end: *Ruft mich morgen an!*

examples.en: Pick me up at the station!

items.explanation: *du schreibst* → remove *-st* → **Schreib** (or *Schreibe*). The Dativ pronoun *mir* (to me) follows the verb directly.

mistake.why: The *-st* ending belongs to the present tense with *du*. In the imperative it disappears: *Schreib mir!*

items.explanation: The *e → i* change of *sprechen* exists only for *du* and *er/sie/es*. For *ihr* the stem is regular: *ihr sprecht* → **Sprecht**.

mistake.why: The infinitive without *Sie* is not an imperative. For a group of friends use the *ihr*-form: *Sprecht!*

items.explanation: *nehmen* changes in the *du*-form: *du nimmst*. Remove *-st* and keep the stem → **Nimm** (with double *m* and short *i*).

mistake.why: *Nehm* is heard in speech, but it is not standard. The *e → i* change stays: *Nimm!*

items.explanation: *trinken* is regular: *du trinkst* → remove *-st* → **Trink**. The object *dein Wasser* shows that you speak to one person you say *du* to.

mistake.why: In the imperative the *-st* ending and the pronoun are dropped: *Trink dein Wasser!*

items.explanation: *helfen* has *e → i* only for *du/er* (*du hilfst*). The *ihr*-form is regular: *ihr helft* → **Helft**. *helfen* takes a Dativ: *mir*.

mistake.why: *hilft* is the *er/sie/es*-form with the vowel change. The *ihr*-imperative keeps *e*: *Helft!*

items.explanation: Formal imperative = infinitive + *Sie*. With the separable verb *zuhören*, only the verb part comes first: **Hören** Sie *zu*! The prefix goes to the end.

mistake.why: The prefix of a separable verb goes to the end, also in the *Sie*-form: *Hören Sie zu!*

items.explanation: The *du*-imperative of *sein* is irregular: **Sei**. It is used with an adjective to tell someone how to behave: *Sei pünktlich!*

mistake.why: The infinitive *sein* is not an imperative. For *du* the form is *Sei!*; only *Sie* has *Seien Sie!*

examples.de: Sei morgen um acht Uhr da!
examples.en: Be there at eight o'clock tomorrow!

items.explanation: Speaking to a group: *ihr geht* → drop *ihr* → **Geht**. The *ihr*-imperative is always the same as the present-tense *ihr*-form.

mistake.why: *gehst* is the *du*-form with *-st*; it is not an imperative at all. For several people the form is *Geht!*

items.explanation: The *du*-imperative is the stem without *-st* and without *du*: **Komm**. *hereinkommen* is separable, so *herein* goes to the end.

mistake.why: The prefix *herein* cannot stay on the verb in position 1. It goes to the end: *Komm bitte herein!*

items.explanation: The formal imperative keeps *Sie* after the infinitive: **Nehmen** Sie. The *e → i* change of *nehmen* never appears with *Sie*. *Platz nehmen* is a fixed polite phrase.

mistake.why: *nimm* is the *du*-imperative. With *Sie* the verb is the infinitive: *Nehmen Sie Platz.*

items.explanation: The *ihr*-imperative is the present tense without *ihr*: *ihr macht* → **Macht**. The possessive *eure* fits: you speak to several people.

mistake.why: The infinitive without *Sie* is not an imperative. *eure* shows that you speak to several people you call *ihr*, so the verb is the *ihr*-form: *Macht!*

items.explanation: *sprechen* keeps the *e → i* change in the *du*-imperative: **Sprich**. A full stop instead of an exclamation mark makes the request sound calmer; the verb form is the same.

mistake.why: The vowel change is right, but the *-st* ending must go: *Sprich bitte langsamer.*

items.explanation: *fahren* has an umlaut in the present (*du fährst*), but the imperative drops it: **Fahr** (or *Fahre*). The negation *nicht* follows the verb.

mistake.why: Unlike *e → i*, the *a → ä* change does not appear in the imperative: *Fahr!*

items.explanation: *sein* has irregular imperatives: **sei** (du), *seid* (ihr), *seien Sie* (Sie). The *du*-form never takes an *-e*.

mistake.why: Many verbs allow an optional *-e* (*komme, gehe*), but *sein* does not: the only *du*-form is *sei*.

items.explanation: The stem of *warten* ends in *-t*. Such verbs need the *-e* in the *du*-imperative: **Warte**. The same applies to *arbeiten → arbeite, antworten → antworte*.

mistake.why: *wartest* is the present-tense *du*-form. The imperative drops *-st* but keeps the *-e*: *Warte!*

items.explanation: *geben → du gibst → **Gib*** (keep *i*, drop *-st*). The Dativ pronoun *mir* comes before the Akkusativ noun *das Salz*.

mistake.why: *Geb* is colloquial, not standard. The *e → i* change stays in the *du*-imperative: *Gib!*

items.explanation: *du stehst auf* → **Steh** … *auf*. The separable prefix *auf* goes to the end, after *bitte* and *früher*.

mistake.why: The prefix *auf* is split off and placed at the end: *Steh bitte früher auf.*

items.explanation: *Angst haben* = to be afraid. The formal imperative is the infinitive + *Sie*: **Haben** Sie. The noun *Angst* is negated with *keine*, not *nicht*.

mistake.why: *habe* is the *du*-imperative (*Hab(e) keine Angst!*). With *Sie* the verb is the infinitive: *Haben Sie …*

items.explanation: *lesen* changes *e → ie*: *du liest*. The imperative keeps *ie* and loses *-t*: **Lies**. No *-e* is added.

mistake.why: Verbs with *e → ie* keep the change and take no *-e* in the imperative: *Lies!*

items.en: Don't forget to switch off the light.
items.focus: du-Imperativ · e → i + Infinitiv mit zu
items.explanation: *vergessen → du vergisst → **Vergiss*** (*e → i*, the double *s* stays). The task follows as a *zu*-infinitive; with the separable verb *ausmachen* the *zu* goes inside: *auszumachen*.

mistake.why: The *e → i* change of *vergessen* stays in the *du*-imperative: *Vergiss!*

examples.en: Don't forget to lock the door.

items.de: {{c1::Setzen::to sit down · wir}} wir uns nach vorne.
items.explanation: The *wir*-imperative (English *let's*) is the infinitive in position 1 + *wir*: **Setzen** wir. The reflexive pronoun *uns* follows *wir*.

mistake.why: The *wir*-imperative keeps the pronoun *wir* after the verb: *Setzen wir uns …*

items.explanation: *du hörst zu* → **Hör** … *zu*. *zuhören* takes the Dativ, so *mir* (not *mich*) stands between the verb and the prefix.

mistake.why: The *du*-imperative has no *-st*: *Hör mir bitte zu.*

items.explanation: *ihr bringt mit* → **Bringt** … *mit*. The prefix *mit* closes the sentence; *etwas zu trinken* (something to drink) stands in the middle.

mistake.why: The prefix *mit* is split off and goes to the end: *Bringt … mit.*

items.explanation: *Entschuldigen Sie …* is a formal imperative (infinitive + *Sie*) used as a fixed polite formula. *die Störung* is the Akkusativ object.

mistake.why: *entschuldigt* is the *ihr*-form. With *Sie* the verb must be the infinitive: *Entschuldigen Sie!*

examples.de: Entschuldigen Sie, wo ist der Bahnhof?
examples.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

items.explanation: The stem *öffn-* ends in consonant + *n*. Such stems need an *-e* to be pronounceable (like *du öffnest*): **Öffne**. The same applies to *atmen → atme*.

mistake.why: *öffn* cannot be pronounced as one syllable. After consonant + *m/n* the *-e* is required: *Öffne!*

items.en: Run quickly, the bus is coming!
items.explanation: *laufen* has an umlaut in the present (*du läufst*), but the imperative uses the infinitive stem: **Lauf**. Like *a → ä*, the change *au → äu* disappears.

mistake.why: Umlaut changes (*ä, äu*) are not used in the imperative. The form is *Lauf!*

examples.en: Go to sleep now, it's late!

items.explanation: *sehen → du siehst*. The imperative keeps *ie* and drops *-st*: **Sieh**. The particle *mal* makes the command friendly and casual.

mistake.why: *sehen* has the *e → ie* change, and it stays in the *du*-imperative: *Sieh mal!*

examples.en: Give me a hand for a moment!

items.explanation: *sein* is the only verb whose *Sie*-imperative is not the infinitive: **Seien** Sie! All other verbs simply use the infinitive (*Haben Sie, Werden Sie*).

mistake.why: *Sind Sie …?* is a question in the present tense. The formal imperative of *sein* is *Seien Sie!*

items.explanation: The *wir*-imperative is the infinitive in position 1 + *wir*: **Fangen** wir. With the separable verb *anfangen*, the prefix *an* goes to the end.

mistake.why: The prefix of a separable verb goes to the end, also in the *wir*-imperative: *Fangen wir jetzt an!*

items.explanation: *haben* forms the *du*-imperative from its stem: **Hab** (or *Habe*). It is not built from *du hast*. The noun *Angst* is negated with *keine*.

mistake.why: *hast* is the present-tense *du*-form. The imperative uses the stem *hab-*: *Hab keine Angst!*

examples.de: Hab keine Sorge, alles ist gut!

items.focus: ihr-Imperativ · Verb mit e → i im Präsens
items.explanation: *nehmen* changes the vowel only for *du/er* (*du nimmst, er nimmt*). The *ihr*-form is regular: *ihr nehmt mit* → **Nehmt** … *mit*.

mistake.why: *nimmt* is the *er/sie/es*-form. The *ihr*-imperative has no vowel change: *Nehmt!*

items.explanation: *du stellst dich vor* → drop *du* and the ending *-st* → **Stell** dich … vor. The pronoun *du* disappears, the reflexive pronoun *dich* stays directly after the verb, and the prefix *vor* goes to the end.

mistake.why: *stellst* is the present-tense *du*-form. The imperative drops the ending *-st*: *Stell dich vor!*

items.explanation: *werden* has *e → i* in the present (*du wirst*), but its imperative is an exception: it keeps *e* and normally takes *-e*: **Werde** (colloquial: *Werd*). It is used mainly in wishes like this one.

mistake.why: *wird* is the *er/sie/es*-form. *werden* does not keep the vowel change in the imperative: *Werde!*

items.en: Please get off at the main station!
items.explanation: Formal imperative = infinitive + *Sie*. With *aussteigen* only *steigen* comes first: **Steigen** Sie … *aus*. The prefix *aus* closes the sentence.

mistake.why: A separable verb is split in the *Sie*-imperative too: *Steigen Sie … aus!*

examples.de: Füllen Sie bitte das Formular aus!

items.explanation: The stem *wart-* ends in *-t*, so the *ihr*-form adds *-et*: *ihr wartet* → **Wartet**. *warten auf* takes the Akkusativ: *auf mich*.

mistake.why: After a stem in *-t* or *-d* an *-e-* is needed before the ending: *wartet, arbeitet, findet*.

items.en: Tell me, how was the holiday?
items.explanation: *erzählen* is regular and has an inseparable prefix: *du erzählst* → **Erzähl**. The particle *mal* makes it a casual invitation rather than an order.

mistake.wrong: Erzählst mal, wie war der Urlaub?
mistake.why: Without the pronoun, *erzählst* is not a command. The *du*-imperative drops *-st*: *Erzähl mal!*

examples.en: Tell me, do you have time?

drills.instruction: Answer the question about forming the *du*-imperative.
drills.prompt: How do you form the *du*-imperative of a regular verb like *kaufen*?
drills.answer: Take the present-tense *du*-form, drop the pronoun and the ending *-st*: *du kaufst → **Kauf!*** An *-e* is optional (*Kaufe!*), but it is required after stems in *-t/-d* and consonant + *m/n*: *Warte! Öffne!*
drills.explanation: In speech the short form without *-e* is normal. The *-e* is required where the stem is hard to pronounce without it: *arbeite, rede, atme, öffne*.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about vowel changes.
drills.prompt: Which present-tense vowel changes stay in the *du*-imperative, and which disappear?
drills.answer: **e → i / ie stays** (*nehmen → nimm, lesen → lies*), and these forms never take *-e*. **a → ä / au → äu disappears** (*fahren → fahr, laufen → lauf*). Exception: *werden → werde*.
drills.explanation: Only *e → i/ie* verbs show the change. Umlaut verbs use the infinitive stem. The *ihr*- and *Sie*-forms never show any vowel change (*nehmt, nehmen Sie*).

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the *ihr*- and *Sie*-forms.
drills.prompt: How do you form the *ihr*-imperative and the *Sie*-imperative?
drills.answer: *ihr*: the present-tense *ihr*-form without *ihr* (*ihr kommt → **Kommt!***). *Sie*: the infinitive + *Sie* (***Kommen Sie!***). *Sie* must always stay; *ihr* is dropped.
drills.explanation: Both forms are regular for almost every verb. Only *sein* is special: *Seid!* and *Seien Sie!* The *wir*-form works like the *Sie*-form: *Gehen wir!* = *Let's go!*

drills.instruction: Answer the question about irregular imperatives.
drills.prompt: What are the imperative forms of *sein* and *haben*?
drills.explanation: *sein* cannot be built from *du bist*, and its *Sie*-form is not the infinitive. *haben* uses the stem *hab-*, not *du hast*. Both are often used with an adjective or noun: *Sei leise! Hab Geduld!*

drills.instruction: Answer the question about word order.
drills.prompt: Where do the verb, a separable prefix and a reflexive pronoun go in an imperative sentence?
drills.answer: The verb is in **position 1**, the separable prefix at the **end**, and a reflexive or object pronoun directly **after the verb** (or after *Sie/wir*): *Zieh dich an! Ruf mich an! Setzen Sie sich!*
drills.explanation: The imperative is a verb-first sentence. The separable verb forms a bracket like in a statement: verb … prefix. Particles like *bitte, mal, doch* stand in the middle.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct form. You speak formally to one person.
drills.answer: Machen Sie bitte das Fenster zu!
drills.explanation: With *Sie* the imperative is the infinitive: *Machen Sie …!* *Mach* is the *du*-form and *Macht* is the *ihr*-form; neither combines with *Sie*.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct form. You speak to a group of children.
drills.explanation: Several children → *ihr*-form: *seid*. *sei* is for one person (*du*), *seien* only works with *Sie*, and *sind* is not an imperative form.

drills.answer: Paul, gib mir bitte das Buch!
drills.explanation: One friend → *du*-imperative. *geben* has *e → i* (*du gibst*), and the change stays: *gib*. *geb* is not standard, *gibst* keeps the *-st*, and *gebt* is for several people.
*isst* is the present-tense *du*-form. The imperative drops the ending: *Iss!* (the double *s* belongs to the stem).
*Ruf* is the *du*-form. With *Sie* the verb must be the infinitive: *Rufen Sie …!*
You speak to one person (Lisa), so you need the *du*-form: *Lauf!* *Lauft* is the *ihr*-form for several people.
Drop *du* and the ending *-st*, and put the verb in position 1: *du kommst → Komm!* The rest of the sentence stays in the same order.

drills.instruction: Change the formal request into a *du*-imperative.
drills.explanation: *helfen* has *e → i* for *du* (*du hilfst*). The *du*-imperative keeps the change and drops *-st* and the pronoun: *Hilf!*

drills.answer: Rufen Sie mich heute Abend an!
drills.explanation: The *Sie*-form is the infinitive *rufen* + *Sie*. The prefix *an* stays at the end, and the object *mich* follows *Sie*.

drills.instruction: Put the parts in the correct order to make a *du*-imperative.
drills.explanation: The verb *mach* comes first and the prefix *an* goes to the end. *Mach die Heizung bitte an!* is also correct; *bitte* can stand before or after the object.

drills.instruction: Put the parts in the correct order to make a *let's*-sentence.
drills.explanation: The *wir*-imperative puts the infinitive first and *wir* second. The particle *doch* follows the pronoun and makes the suggestion sound friendly.
